newsitem.title: FRANCE: Euro-MPs welcome new sex discrimination laws.
newsitem.headline: Euro-MPs welcome new sex discrimination laws.

text.p: Plans for European Union rules to give women better protection against discrimination at work won resounding support from the European Parliament on Thursday.
The European Commission is proposing a binding EU-wide directive which would shift the burden of proof in sex discrimination cases away from women and onto their employers.

Euro-MPs followed the advice of Italian Socialist rapporteur Fiorella Ghilardotti and introduced amendments designed to strengthen the Commission text, the majority of which have received the backing of European Social Commissioner Padraig Flynn.
Among these include a more precise definition of "indirect discrimination" and a call for the law to come into effect on at the start of 2000, rather than a year later.

The EU treaty (Article 119) and six EU directives set a clear legal basis for equal pay and equal treatment between men and women, reinforced by a considerable volume of case law in the European Court of Justice.
"Yet in spite of this," says Ghilardotti's report, "women continue to suffer discrimination, both in the workplace and in society as a whole."
This is evidenced, she explains, "by the continuing large difference in average pay between men and women in all (EU) member states and the low percentage of women in decision-making positions."
One of the main difficulties is actually proving discrimination has taken place.

The Commission has tried in the past to shift the burden of proof but an attempt in 1998 to change the law and make it easier for women to bring a case by placing the onus to prove that discrimination failed to win the necessary unanimous support from EU social ministers.

In its latest proposal -- COM(96)340 -- the Commission says that once the courts have accepted a woman's claim that there is a case to answer, then it is up to the employer to prove that discrimination has not occurred.

Parliament agreed that by shifting the burden of proof the proposal would make it easier to bring discrimination cases to court and thus help build up a body of case law which would provide a clear legal basis for future cases.
The proposal is based on the social protocol to the EU treaty, which does not apply to Britain.
Commissioner Flynn told Euro-MPs on Wednesday he would put pressure on EU ministers to accept several of parliament's amendments.
He said social ministers would not be asked to approve the proposal before June, giving plenty of time for them to consider parliament's amendments.
The draft directive must have the support of both parliament and ministers before it can become law.
